BOSS Audio Systems 625UAB Multimedia Car Stereo - Bluetooth Audio And Hands Free Calling, Single Din, MP3 Player, No CD/DVD Player, USB Port, AUX Input, AM/FM Radio Receiver, Detachable Face This car stereo exceeded all of my expectations. True, those expectations were super low due to how inexpensive this is. But, my goodness, it was nice to get a good surprise for a change.

But then came the bad surprise: one night, we started the car, and the blue lights came on but the stereo did not. It wouldn't turn on. It wouldn't turn off. And when the car sat for a day, it drained the battery dry.

Which fixed it. It needed to have the power cut completely in order to reset. Your mileage may vary, but for me, that's a nonstarter. Get it? The husband thinks it's no big deal, at least not worth replacing until it quits entirely. He's the installer, so he wins.

The sound is perfectly serviceable. It gets loud, and all frequencies are clear. Bluetooth connection works great, though my husband prefers aux in for sound quality (Mr. Ears). It was an easy install in my 2004 Odyssey EX (I bought a wiring harness and a frame kit). Still, I would not buy it again.

Three and a half stars.
text_fidelity_b: BOSS Audio Systems 625UAB Multimedia Car Stereo - Bluetooth Audio And Hands Free Calling, Single Din, MP3 Player, No CD/DVD Player, USB Port, AUX Input, AM/FM Radio Receiver, Detachable Face

text_fidelity_a:
Canon PowerShot SX500 IS 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 30x Wide-Angle Optical Image Stabilized Zoom and 3.0-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL) I recently took this camera, along with my PowerShot Elph 110, on a Caribbean cruise. Because I have the waterproof case for the 110, I used it whenever I was shooting in wet areas and also for underwater shots. I used the SX500 in dry locations. In some instances, I was able to take comparable shots with both cameras and the difference was really striking. Let me preface this by saying that I'm NOT a photographer. I'm just someone who likes to take a lot of pictures. I like them to come out well, but I know virtually nothing about photography beyond what I've learned through trial and error.

I found the low-light shots taken with the SX500 to be FAR superior than those taken with the Elph. Yes, it's difficult to capture a moving subject in low light. This isn't and expensive, professional camera. I'm very pleased with the results considering the price I paid.

The biggest selling feature was the zoom lens. I was absolutely AMAZED how clear shots taken from VERY far away came out. I took this camera to Opening Day, to see the Red Sox players get their World Series rings. We didn't have the best of seats, so I had to really max out the zoom lens. I was certain the photos would be blurry. It's difficult to hold a camera really still, extremely zoomed in, while standing in a crowd. The photos were OUTSTANDING. I mean really...outstanding!

I'm extremely pleased with this purchase. The camera is small and easy to carry with the strap around my neck. When I want something I can slip in my pocket, I opt for the Elph.

I would classify this as a bridge camera. It's NOT as easy to carry around as a pocket-sized digital, but it's also not as cumbersome to carry around as a more professional model. It's EASY to use...even for novices like me! And it takes great photos. I'm sure as I have more trial-and-error lessons under my belt, my shots will be even better.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SX500 IS 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 30x Wide-Angle Optical Image Stabilized Zoom and 3.0-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a: ASUS C200 Chromebook 11.6 Inch (Intel Celeron, 2 GB, 16GB SSD, Black/Silver) I have an aging netbook that isn't really worth turning on anymore, and wanted a portable solution with a keyboard.  Unfortunately, the netbook market kinda died, but then again, the Chromebooks have seem to come into their own.  As a fan of ASUS's products, I couldn't turn this little guy down, especially at this price.  Over all, the build quality feels solid.  It's obviously plastic, but the construction is solid.  The screen on this Chromebook is serviceable, but has limited viewing angles.  Netflix and Amazon Prime videos seem to stream just fine.  The biggest surprise for me is the keyboard and touch pad.  Normally I have a hard time with touch pads, but this one is great!  And the keyboard feels like it belongs on a computer that cost 3 or 4 times as much (I own a $1000 ASUS gaming laptop.)  When it comes to performance, I do question how long this will last...  Scrolling though webpages isn't as smooth as it would be on a decent laptop, and I know that the guts of this machine aren't meant for high performance.  Regardless, this is definitely worth purchasing for convenience and portability!
text_fidelity_b: ASUS C200 Chromebook 11.6 Inch (Intel Celeron, 2 GB, 16GB SSD, Black/Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
turelar Compatible Headphone Jack Dongle Adapter for Phone X 8/8plus 7/7plus I received a review copy of this receiver and put it through its paces. I am going to compare it to a receiver that I've owned since 2011 and have been thoroughly pleased with: [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]].

It's a complete solution: the box contained easy-to-follow instructions and two sets of cables: one 3.5mm male at each end and the other with a 3.5mm male splitting into two RCA males. Those are a nice touch because some speakers require one or the other. With my Belkin I had to purchase an adapter to use it with one of my powered speakers. So having a complete solution right out of the box is a plus.

The receiver looks like a wall wart that plugs directly into a wall socket. It's about two inches tall and 1.75 inches wide, so it does eat up come space. Since the speaker cable comes out the bottom of the device you are pretty much locked into plugging it into the bottom receptacle.

One feature I loved is this also has a port for USB charging that allows you to keep your phone or MP3 player fully charged while playing music.

This, of course, is based on later technology and it shows. I greatly exceeded the ten meter distance limit by taking my phone to the opposite end of my house, two rooms apart from the receiver, and still managed a clear signal. Believe me, on its best day the Belkin struggled to receive a line of sight signal within a ten meter limit. I even took my phone outside and could hear clear reception coming from my speakers inside my house.

While the instruction sheet will step you through connecting to and using this receiver I did not bother to read it. I opened the bluetooth settings on my [[ASIN:B00AB7FVCY Samsung Galaxy Note II]], scanned for new devices and when BrightPlay Home showed up in the list I tapped it to connect and started streaming music to my speaker. It took longer to unpackage the receiver than it did to start using it. It does not get any easier.

The sound quality is markedly better too. I switched back and forth between the Belkin receiver and this one - attached to the same powered speakers - and could tell the difference. Not by much, mind you, but it's discernible. I had a friend listen and she agreed.

Overall this is an excellent receiver that exceeded the recommended specs in the instruction sheet and it a breeze to use. If I had to replace this it would be with an identical receiver and that is the highest praise I can bestow.
text_fidelity_b: turelar Compatible Headphone Jack Dongle Adapter for Phone X 8/8plus 7/7plus

VANGUARD GH-200 Tripod Heads This is a sturdy tripod head, ideal for serious photographers shooting HDR images, panoramas and sporting events.

Pros:
1. Holds DSLR cameras and lenses firmly
2. The shoe slides into place easily and is secured by a knob lock and safety stops.
3. Simple system to rotate and adjust, with two spirit levels for portrait and landscape shots.
4. 360 degree rotation for very smooth and easy panning

Cons:
1. "Quick" shoe isn't that quick as you have to find a coin or screwdriver to attach it to your camera.
2. It's not easy to use if you have small hands - it isn't physically possible for me to use the Grip Position Release System with one hand.
3. The trigger action is very stiff and makes my hands tired very quickly
4. Adds significantly to the weight of the tripod

I use this mostly for motor sports events and panoramas because of the smooth panning action, where I don't need to move around much or pull the trigger very often. This would probably work a lot better in the hands of a stronger person with bigger hands.

text_fidelity_a: Western Digital 2TB WD Blue SN570 NVMe Internal Solid State Drive SSD - Gen3 x4 PCIe 8Gb/s, M.2 2280, Up to 3,500 MB/s - WDS200T3B0C Our budget Lenovo (IdeaPad 3 15IIL05) came with a 256GB SSD. To make it more useful, I originally paired it with an external WD Black 500 GB hdd. That has its limitations, though, as it's not very transportable. After the warranty expired, upgrading to the 1 TB internal SSD was simple. Lots of online videos on how to remove the back cover and locate the SSD. First I took the new SSD and put it into an SSD enclosure I also purchased on Amazon. Then I was able to format it with Windows from the existing SSD (hidden partition). Finally I removed the laptop cover, took the old SSD out and put the new SSD in. The old SSD went into the SSD external enclosure. It was easy to copy all the files from the external hdd to the new 1 TB drive, and I've been up and running with no issues. No problems with portability, either (the 500GB hdd is semi-retired; I only pull it out on rare occassions). Great upgrade!

Tablet 10 inch Android 10.0 4G LTE Tablet PC with 2 SIM Card Slot 4GB RAM 64GB ROM 128GB Expandable Octa Core 1.6GHz 1280x800 IPS 1080P FHD SD Type-C 6000mAh 13 MP Camera Bluetooth WiFi GPS OTG, Gray [[VIDEOID:bb1b31acd3cedf3d01bf5f12246299fd]] THE GOOD:
--------------
* Budget tablet with a lot of bells and whistles such as: Octa core cpu, 4gb of ram, and sim card feature to use your cell phone services.
* 4gb of ram allows the tablet to be quite responsive.
* 64gb of storage, but SD slot can take an additional 128gb card.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Build quality, but keep in mind you're talking about a sub $150 tablet. Watch my video, towards the end you see me squeeze parts of the tablets, you can hear a lot of creaking. Tell-tale sign of a cheap build.
* Wifi goes dead every day. We're not talking drop connections, we're talking completely gone. Even if you toggle the wifi back on, it just goes gray. The good news is that all it takes is a restart to fix it, and since the tablet is pretty fast, the restart is fast too. Another good news is that, it doesn't seem to go dead while you're online. I think it is when it's been sleeping for awhile, that's when it can vanish. Weird.

My son's Fire HD 10 broke, and we were out of our warranty period. So he's been using this tablet. For games such as Roblox, Among Us, etc., this tablet is very responsive. He hasn't complained to me about lag. Something he complains a lot with his Fire HD. The wifi issue is the biggest negative. But like I mentioned above, the wifi seems to only go bad if the tablet has been inactive for awhile. We'll rate this tablet 3-Stars. They fix the wifi issue, it would be 5-Stars for a budget tablet.

After a ton of research, my tech hubby decided the newest version of the Nexus still meet our needs the best. We've only had this one 3 months, but so far so good.
Our old Nexus experience:
The first nexus we bought survived my sons' toddlerhood very well!. My husband bought it two and a half years ago for reading in bed. Our son had just turned two. My husband wiped the old Nexus clean and it did help speed it up quite a bit... so it is now perfect for our 18month old daughter, since toddler apps don't require much space or the latest software. She can't really "play" any of the apps yet. All she really can do at this age is "color" on it.... but she's had the old one for three months and beats the ever loving cr*p out of it on a daily basis... and it's still going strong. There isn't a scratch on the screen. IDK, I'm just very impressed with Nexus, seeing as how every time one of my adult friends drop their iPhone, I see them ranting on facebook about how it shattered instantly.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) “I wonder how long it has been we readers have gazed at the young person sitting under a tree at night reading a book on the Kindle home screen..oh, our love affair with books and being able to read our stories late into the night…...by candlelight….anywhere.”

Pre-release technology reviewers commenting on the price of the Kindle Oasis are wrong. The new Kindle Oasis is worth the the price Amazon is charging, including cover it hardly represents at all an increase in price when compared with a Kindle Voyage with cover. Yet it provides the two most asked for improvements in mobile devices: increased battery life reducing the need to frequently recharge, and improved screen legibility (new sans-serif Ember font, and more LEDS that provide increased brightness).

“When we are immersed into the story of our favorite books, only that world matters.”

Pre-release technology reviewers have compared the Kindle as a single purpose e-reader, to multipurpose devices like in smartphones, tablets and computers. When we choose to read, we are seeking a bit of solitude in the day and night. Oh, how easy it is to remember being annoyed with yet another incoming phone call, text message or email. The power of focus!

“The tactile feel of a book”

Pre-release technology reviewer have labelled the Kindle as luxurious with it’s leather cover. How soon we forget our books covered with leather! And we are willing to pay an extra price for it!

As I sit across the street from the one and only Amazon retail store “in the world”, I have unboxed and set up my new Kindle Oasis. Maybe I am one of the few ordinary people outside of Amazon and the technology press in the world to have been able to purchase one so soon. The feeling reminds me of going to a release party in the same shopping center for the latest Harry Potter novel.

This Kindle is new, like the latest release from our favorite author.

It connects me to reading anywhere, late at night when there is little light.

The Kindle Oasis is magical.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

text_fidelity_a:
Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10 You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10

I own about a dozen radios that cost around $400 each. They are incredibly high quality and obviously very expensive too. But they are not the kind of radios you would camp or backpack with. They are too heavy and large for that application.

So, I did my research and bought these Midland radios. AND THEY ARE GREAT!! They have a clear and strong signal under reasonable conditions for ANY radio. Some of these reviews that whine about range clearly don't understand how radios work. They are not cell phones using giant towers that carry your signal across the nation. Radios--whether they are $400 each or $40 each, cannot overcome solid obstacles like houses and trees and mountains indefinitely. I was impressed at how well these did under less than ideal conditions.

Ignore these reviewers that have unattainable standards and get these radios.

text_fidelity_a:
iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice This is a pretty mixed review of an interesting concept that is pretty good right now, but has the potential to be great in the near future. At the current price of about $150, this is ok+ based on the following criteria:

Sound Quality: 2.5-3 stars
For the size, it's ok
When reviewing for sound quality, I compare speakers (and headphones) to comparably sized items, based on speakers I currently or previously have owned. I take price range *somewhat* into account (I don't expect $15 headphones to sound like $500 ones), but for anything over $100, I use the full range from the cheapest stuff I have, to my favorite brand, Bose.
So with that in mind, I have a portable wireless Bose speaker that is smaller and acts as the "5" on the scale.
The sound on this can get loud enough to not distort and still fill a smallish room or normal bedroom fine. The treble and bass are ok, though the higher ranges are tinny and the bass lacks depth. Overall sound from high to low and throughout the mid range lack definition. It's good enough for very casual background listening and for podcasts.

Alexa Feature: 4 stars
I have an iPhone and think Alexa has quite a bit more understanding and skill than Siri. When asked questions, from simple stuff like "what's the weather" to more complicated stuff like "I'm hungry. What can I make in half an hour?", the answers and follow-up questions are highly intuitive and thorough. Does she get everything all the time? No. But she does a much better job than Siri.

User-Friendliness: 2.5 stars
I didn't like the process of figuring out how this works, particularly the part of pairing with more than one device and also Having to use an app to make most of it work. It was a clunky, irritating process that more or less stayed that way every time I wanted to use this thing, especially for listening to music. It should be able to just play from your iTunes through the iTunes app and bluetooth, and instead, I was only able to make it play iTunes though Their App, which sucks when it comes to my music. And that brings us to the App..

App: 2 stars
No. Just no. Bluetooth exists for a reason, and if a speaker has bluetooth, you should be able to just pair and play. I had to use the app to play from my iTunes, and because I have a very specific way of organizing things, I was incredibly annoyed that something didn't translate, and my music was disorganized and basically impossible to search for with this app. Instead of being able to play what I want from one of my playlist subfolders, it disregarded my way of organizing things, and I ended up giving up. If I can't listen to my stuff easily with this, then like 75% of the reason to use this disappears, leaving me with an expensive alarm clock with weather report, recipe ideas, and some cool internet stuff. That's cool, but it's quite incomplete for what I need, and what I suspect many people want.

tl;dr version: sound is mediocre but doable, app is bad, Alexa is super clever and smart, and the experience has a lot of frustrating aspects.
text_fidelity_b: iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice

HUION Keydial Mini Bluetooth Programmable Keypad with Dial 5 Keys Anti-ghosting 18 Customized Keys, Wireless Shortcut Keyboard for Drawing Tablet, PC, MacBook, Surface Pro, Laptops I'm no artist in any way but I do want to try getting into digital art. As a present to myself, I purchased the [[ASIN:B083W88L5H Huion Kamvas 13]] to get started. Huion is known for providing great quality in their products while keeping the prices affordable.

As anyone who has used a drawing tablet can attest, with the tablet taking up the main desk space, it's difficult to access the keyboard for all the shortcut keys that help to make the job easier. One option is to use an under-the-desk keyboard tray, but I really don't like doing that as I tend to kick the tray when I get in and out of my chair. Others purchase more expensive hotkey devices such as this one.

While the HUION Mini KeyDial KD100 does not have fancy led lights or e-ink display on the keys, it does have the basics of what one would need. The keys are laid out like the number pad on a full 101-key keyboard and the dial can be used to adjust anything that needs a kind of analog input (volume, zoom, brush size, etc). The keys are preconfigured for the most common shortcuts but each key can be customized.

The Mini KeyDial came in an oddly plain white box with the name Huion printed on top. It's almost like this is a rebranded white-box device but that really isn't a problem. It simply means that the unboxing experience isn't as satisfying as the drawing tablet itself. Once connected to the Huion drivers, the device feels fully integrated to Huion's ecosystem.

It is managed in the same driver/software that Huion uses for its tablets so that once you'll be able to get up and running customizing the buttons immediately.

Last thing to point out is that the dial on this device can support Microsoft's own RaDial drivers to emulate the dial that Microsoft introduced a few years ago for the Surface Studio, allowing it to interact natively with built-in Windows utilities.
text_fidelity_b: HUION Keydial Mini Bluetooth Programmable Keypad with Dial 5 Keys Anti-ghosting 18 Customized Keys, Wireless Shortcut Keyboard for Drawing Tablet, PC, MacBook, Surface Pro, Laptops

Connected to a USB 2.0 port on an older desktop PC, it’s slightly faster than a darned good internal TP-Link adapter. Connected to a USB 3.0 port on that same PC, it’s about 25 Mbps faster, delivering downloads at an average 225+ Mbps. (Comcast delivers very high Internet speeds on the adapters’ second bands, where there is far less Internet traffic.)

A nice thing about this adapter is that you can move it around, and aim it, so that it picks up the very best wi-fi signal from your router. It comes with the option of installing a software package for managing the adapter, or installing a standalone driver if you want to continue using a different connection manager. If you install the software package, you get an easy-to-use Genie program that tells you whether the adapter is connected, what its MAC number is, etc.

I’m a major fan of Netgear products (routers and adapters). In my experience, Netgear products deliver as advertised, are stable and trouble-free, and last for years.

I really like the ability to charge these with the QI charger I have. That makes it convenient to charge at not android users houses. The manual does a good job of explaining what tapping the side will do and you can also power them on and off holding down the side of it.

text_fidelity_a: Swimbuds Sport Premium Waterproof Headphones & 11 eartips in 4 Styles (Upgraded Cord) This is my second pair of Swimbuds. I've always struggled finding headphones that would not leak while swimming.  It must be some anatomical issue with my ear canal, because I've tried at least a dozen headphones - and all of them leaked or fell out at some point.  These swim buds are so light that they actually stay in my ear.  Short cord doesn't get tangled up.  And I guess the Christmas-tree tips are a bit different because so far these headphones are the only one that have not leaked, but I do have to insert them deep into ear canal.  I use just a touch of petroleum jelly on tips to help the insertion and to moisturise ears, because these headphones (like most other waterproof headphones) can cause irritation of the external ear canal.  There are a lot of tips to choose from.  I use them in my Endless Pool, so I don't know how they will perform in regular pool during turns and flips, but my guess is because of their lightness they will work fine.  I don't care much for clarity of music during swimming, but I found sound to be quite acceptable with these headphones.
text_fidelity_b: Swimbuds Sport Premium Waterproof Headphones & 11 eartips in 4 Styles (Upgraded Cord)

Targus Vuscape Case and Stand for iPad mini (fits iPad mini 1, 2, 3) Black (THZ182US) The Targus VuScape Protective cover and stand is a pretty good, helpful aid for those who own an Apple Ipad2. It features a thin, lightweight design that is meant to hold the iPad2 snugly in place while you work.

Having a stand for your iPad is certainly a good idea and I like that this stand can be used to position your iPad in different ways. There are multiple grooves so that you can display your iPad at different angles. The cover can also be folded back completely, allowing the consumer to hold the iPad in the hands without the stand.

This protective cover/stand does have some nice features to offer, but after using it for a while, it is more than apparent that the stand is not perfect. Probably the greatest issue is that the stand isn't as sturdy as I would prefer. If you use the stand on a solid, flat surface, you shouldn't have too many problems, but place it on other surfaces and it tends to bend just a little bit. The slightest bend will cause the grooves to give way just a little, and the iPad will no longer be securely held in place.

I generally like the thin, lightweight design of this stand, but the thinness possibly goes a tad far. If the manufacturer had made this stand just a little bit thicker, it would be stronger and more likely to hold the iPad in place without any problems. I suppose this is the trade- off one must make when selecting a stand such as this. Lightweight is nice, especially for something like an iPad, but lightweight means the stand is lacking in strength.

All in all, this is a good stand and certainly worth considering, but not a deluxe stand like I expected. Again, as long as you are willing to sacrifice sturdiness for lightweight design, you should be fine. And try to use only on the flattest surfaces for the best results. Follow these guidelines and you should find yourself reasonably happy with this protective cover and stand from Targus.
text_fidelity_b: Targus Vuscape Case and Stand for iPad mini (fits iPad mini 1, 2, 3) Black (THZ182US)

The RCA protector plugs into one three-prong outlet, with a plastic support pin that's intended to slot into the ground hole of a lower outlet. text_fidelity_a:
Logitech 910000153 V220 Cordless Optical Mouse for Notebooks [[VIDEOID:c6148faf689d084cd73b4a5362755ed1]] Just playing around with my first ever video review, so please bear with me.

The V220 is a pretty good mouse considering the price tag. It's compact and rugged looking, with rubber pads at the sides for a good grip.

It only needs one AA battery (Note: the diagram is misleading with regard to the way to put in the battery. You should see the + side when you're closing the top)

You can use it for desktops as well as laptops.

There's storage space for the receiver at the bottom, and once you click it into place, the mouse automatically shuts off.

The ridged rubber wheel is the noisy variety, and goes click, click, click, all the way home.

It comes with no software, but gives you a link to the website where you can get a download to make the mouse do tricks. After the download, you can scroll from side to side, click and roll to zoom, and if you give it a shove, it can even roll over and play dead.

It has a warning light to tell you when your battery needs changing.

It doesn't come with a case or pouch, but looks like it can handle going commando just fine.

In summary, it's a good mouse, but not a great mouse - and well worth the price.

Amanda Richards, October 9, 2007
text_fidelity_b: Logitech 910000153 V220 Cordless Optical Mouse for Notebooks

co2CREA Hard Case with Sleep Mode Replacement for Apple AirPods Max Headphone (Black Case + Inside Red) First, mine didn’t smell.

Now that I have the positive attributes out of the way let’s discuss why you should avoid this case.
I reluctantly paid $33 for this and I have to wonder what I was thinking. It’s nowhere near worth that much.

It will not/cannot survive a side impact. Well that’s not true. It cannot protect your APM from a hit or drop that could damage them from the top. I’m not sure if it could from the bottom or sides. It’s either molded cardboard or thin plastic covered with fabric. No padding, just fabric.

Internally there is another layer of cardboard (or plastic, thin, very thin) covered in a felt like material. There’s absolutely no drop protection.

The magnets designed to put the APM into “sleep” mode lay flat. You will have to pinch them up while putting your headphones into it if you wish to keep them from clanging together and not using the stock case. Even then the magnets don’t work every time. See my pic.

Overall this is a $10 case marked up cause they can. I mean we have expensive headphones so why not charge us more? We have already proven we will pay.

Skip this thing. Mine is going back. If you want something to protect them in a backpack then still look elsewhere. You can get something equal to this for less.

Thanks for your time.

text_fidelity_a:
Mostof Dual Ring Light with Stand, Mirror, Phone Holder, Remote, for TikTok YouTube Live Stream Makeup Selfie Photography So ... 2020 .... what do you think of it so far? Our meetings for worship have been moved to Zoom online. So we are are video conferencing multiple times a week. The lighting in our office and on my Mac is great. But for those meetings we use my husband's window's based, 5 year old laptop, out in the kitchen because it runs one of the secondary programs we need to use. The lighting is just "meh". I have been trying to find a good lighting source and have tried and returned a few products out of my own pocket.

This system is a keeper. I little cumbersome, a little top heavy, a little cheap feeling in some respects, but lighting wise, when you get it adjusted is quite nice. Us personally, we look a little more like real people with better lighting.

I have included a before and after picture. I am not a selfie taker, just a pushing 50 year old, middle aged woman, so bear with my picture, I just tried to give you an idea of what some light and color adjustments can do.

Ours is set with a red filter. That seemed to work best for our laptop camera. It is set to medium brightness. Ours is extended over us with the round lights facing more downward and out of our eyes. They are positioned more over the laptop than near us and maybe a foot above the laptop. There is more play for extension with the unit, but that is what works for us.

It comes with mirrors and phone holders, etc etc. We don't use any of that right now but it gives you options. The round mirror head which the the two lights screw on to is flimsy. I would not be surprised if it breaks eventually. The weight of the lights on the small screw in assembly just don't seem like someone thought this all the way through with gravity and weight. So be forewarned. That could be improved.

Overall ... finally a lighting system that works and is pretty simple to set up. Any regrets? Actually no! Would I recommend? Yes. This definitely has a place in today's zoom, tiktok, instagram, youtubey saavy world of Influencers, and also for those of us joe-schmoes who just need better lighting.
text_fidelity_b: Mostof Dual Ring Light with Stand, Mirror, Phone Holder, Remote, for TikTok YouTube Live Stream Makeup Selfie Photography

First of all, it came much larger than I expected it to be. It's also very nice looking and seems to be well made. We have a small one that's made of plastic, but the fabric accent on this one looks nice. The only thing I know how to do is hook my firestick up to it, and that was extremely easy to do. The picture looks great and the sound is much better quality than the smaller one that I have. The smaller one requires an extra speaker just to hear anything, whereas with this one we can easily hear it in our living room and in much of the house. It came with a bag to store it in, but I just repack it exactly the way it came and put it away in the box when we won't be using it.
It may not look and sound as great as going to the movie theater, but it's a fun alternative, as you can eat what you want, wear what you want, and be right in the comfort of your own home while enjoying a great movie with your family or friends.
This FANGOR 701 Video Projector provides a great entertaining experience for me and my family and friends, especially for me and my grandkids. Really, that's all I need it to do. I'm not sure what the price point is, so I can't comment on that. But, I would definitely recommend it!

This cable is dual link which allows resolutions up to 1920 × 1200. It is also 9.8 ft. Cable lengths up to 15 feet will work for this resolution.
This cable is pinned for digital only, no analog, and is used for flat panel displays, digital CRT displays, projectors, HDTV and Video Projectors. Most new high resolution monitors come with HDMI ports. These cables are similar except that HDMI also carries audio signals.
These cables are a high quality, gold plated which reduces the chance of oxidation as long as you don't damage them.

text_fidelity_a:
Michael Kors Lexington 2 Smartwatch - Black Stainless Steel If you like fully featured smart watches, it is hard to find anything this watch can't do! It runs Google's Wear OS, which is their watch variation of Android, so Google users should feel right at home with it. It's got a Play Store for apps, a really fluid interface, and of course it integrates really well with an Android Smartphone. I've been told it doesn't play as nicely with iPhones, but a lot of the core features are standardized and cross platform so it can still function as a really nice watch and allow notifications and call support regardless of device.
My wife had a Fossil Wear OS watch previously, and the feature set is very similar except for one huge plus this has: A SPEAKER! Many of the third party entry level Wear OS watches have a microphone for digital assistant commands and voice-to-text typing, but lack a speaker for it to talk back. So you have to read your responses on the screen and you can't exactly take phone calls. But THIS ONE DOES! Thanks to the speaker, you can full on take calls like a modern day Dick Tracy. That's really useful and cool, especially if you put your phone down or have it in a pocket you don't want to pull it out of all the time.
But here's the big con:
BATTERY LIFE. While this is better than other wear OS watches I've tried, it seems like Wear OS is so feature-filled, they generally need to be charged as often as smartphones do. Battery obviously depends on usage, but average use seems to last about a day or two at a time. Heavy usage and you'll need to top it off every night at least. This isn't the fault of this watch, but rather Wear OS in general. Other smart watches such as the Samsungs and FitBits can go for days to nearly a week on a charge, which means you not only won't have to worry about charging it more than once or twice a week, but you also can do sleep tracking and just leave it on at night. That's something I'm trying to do in order to have healthier sleeping habits. Some devices such as the Mi Band and Amazefit can go for around 20 days on a charge! I was using a Mi Band 3 before trying this watch, and while it doesn't run apps or have a full color screen or take phone calls, I think I prefer having a watch that only needs to be charged about once a month, and can show me my sleeping data as well as pedometer and activity charts, all while alerting me to notifications. I feel like Wear OS has a ways to go before I'm ready to switch over full time. The good news is that devices ARE getting better, as this shows. If you love Wear OS and the smartest features available, this is a good option. But personally I think I'm going back to my "smartwatch lite" that has less bells and whistles but actually fits better functionally into my life.
I want to give this 3.5 stars, I feel like 3 is too low because it IS good for what it is, but I also don't like it enough to use it daily. So settling on 4.

ASUS N900 WiFi Router (RT-N66U) - Dual Band Gigabit Wireless Internet Router, 4 GB Ports, Gaming & Streaming, Easy Setup, Parental Control After searching review after review for a router with solid performance and features I ended up with the N66. I am not a networking professional but I can tell you there is an enormous difference between a good N900 router and an N300 router you may have gotten from your ISP. I would take any review that is not written by a professional with a grain of salt but here's my 2 cents.

I live in a densely populated area with 20+ Wi-Fi networks with decent strength AND I live in a brick building. I have 50 Mps/down from my ISP and with this router I am able maintain at least 50 Mps throughout my ~900 ft2 apartment with one exception, the back porch. Speeds dip to about 15 Mps on the back porch on both the 2.4 & 5 Ghz bands, as I understand it Wi-Fi doesn't get along with brick. There is a brick wall in between my the rest my house and and finally my router. Understandable.

The takeaway, if you need a fast router, I think you will be hard pressed to find a better one. I haven't even touched on USB support for printers, USB applications & external storage, VPN, iOS applications, etc.

text_fidelity_a: SABRENT USB 3.0 Tool Free Enclosure for 2.5” and 3.5” Internal SATA Hard Drives (EC-KSL3) I was all set to return this because it would not recognize my Seagate 4TB SSHD. In disk management it showed up as GPT protective partition. After googling, I found that the only way to get past this was to use Diskpart and Clean the drive--that meant wiping out everything on the drive. Since I had already cloned it, I went ahead and used the Clean command and wiped it out. Still couldn't do anything with the drive in disk management. So using Diskpart again, I used the command, Create Partition Primary. At this point, Diskpart couldn't do anything else. It would not create a volume to format, so I had to use Disk Management to create the volume and format it to exFat. I should state that the drive was recognized by my computer internally when it was connected to a Sata port, but once it was put into the Sabrent, it's drive information was changed and made unusable until I performed the procedure above. Not sure why this happened, maybe because it's a SSHD, but I kinda doubt it since I had no problems with the drive when connected to a Sata Port.
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT USB 3.0 Tool Free Enclosure for 2.5” and 3.5” Internal SATA Hard Drives (EC-KSL3)

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included First I like sound! I'm an audiophile at heart but in my life now I'm an audiophile on a BUDGET! These are my first bluetooth speakers. More on that in a minute.

I was looking for on ear bluetooth speakers with a budget of about $50 to $60 and was set on waiting for a sale on the JBL EB45T but then saw these recommended on the wirecutter website (a pretty good review site in my opinion)

There is nothing wrong with these, but nothing really right about them either. They have a nice neutral sound that you can listen to for a long time. For movies and youtube on my computer, they are great. But there is nothing in the sound that is going to wow you either. Trust me if there was something actually wrong with the sound, I'd be telling you. You can listen to these for a long time without ear fatigue. If you are looking for lots of rumble for movies, these probably aren't the right phones for you. But if your movie listening requirements are more modest then these work well for that. For casual background music, podcasts, audiobooks, they will work really well for that.

Isolation is not great. I think the plastic is thin so a certain amount of noise gets in. I wanted to be able to hear a little bit of background noise, things going on in the house, but these push my limit for how much I want to hear. Even though they were open-back my Sennheiser HD-229 did a better job with isolation because of the design of the pad.

Comfort isn't bad and for my ears, the ear cup size is just about right size. I wish the earpieces swiveled a bit more but for my head, they swivel just enough. . They have a left and right and the cups swivel so little that if you have them on the wrong way you will notice.

Bluetooth... These are a pain in the backside on Win 7. When I want to use them I have to go and delete the previous pairing, pair them again and then go to the control panel and set these to be used for output. For movies on the computer, they get out of sync. I even set my movie player (Pot Player which I highly recommend) to use the Bluetooth headphones and they still get out of sync with the audio. I don't know if it's the player, the USB Bluetooth adapter, Windows 7 or some combination of them together.

I like that they can be used with a wire as well as with bluetooth. The controls are a little small, as mentioned by others but I don't have trouble working them.

I also tried the JBL EB45T Bluetooth headphones, which cost almost twice as much, at Target and these sound better overall. The JBL might have had better highs, a little punchier bass but these are more cohesive across the frequency range with nothing tweaked to make them sound 'better'.

Summary: I don't have any other Bluetooth headphones to compare these to but I think most people would be very satisfied with these at this price point for general use. If however, you are looking for audiophile on a budget, it's not here.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included

Donner Noise Cancelling Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.2 Earphones with 4 Mic Clear Calls, 12mm Drivers, App for Custom EQ, 32H Playtime, Fast Charging, Transparency - Dobuds ONE, Blue Budget-priced earbuds are complicated to review because, in my experience, all $200 earbuds sound significantly better than all $50 earbuds, but there is still a lot of demand for value-priced "good enough" products. I do own a couple of $200 earbuds and they do sound noticeably richer and clearer than these $40 earbuds. However, when I'm out jogging or traveling (eg airplane or train) or listening to voice podcasts, having the absolute best sound quality isn't really important to me. In those situations, features are more important to me, like active noise cancellation, equalization, good volume, good battery life, and easy access to the features. I'd rather use cheap earbuds that I don't mind losing somewhere along the way.

These earbuds have average quality sound for the $40 price. Where these Donner earbuds beat the competition is the features. I've never owned $40 earbuds with app control before. The user manual has a QR code to let you download the app. The QR code did not work, but I did find the "Donner Control" app in the Google Play app store and the app works fine on my Android phone. The app lets me pick from pre-programmed equalization settings or design my own. Adjusting the equalization for different types of music makes a significant difference in audio clarity. The app also lets me choose from 3 active noise cancellation modes. These features don't work as well as in $200 earbuds, but these are $40 earbuds and most $40 earbuds don't have any of these features or any app at all. You can control some of these features with the confusing set of triple-tap commands on the earbuds, but I can never remember those and would rather just tap the picture in the app.

The app also lets you download firmware updates from Donner. None was available when I checked, but this could be a great way for them to refine the features of the earbuds or even add new features. They ask you to give them your email address and create an account when you open the app, but I did not and the core features of the app still work OK.

Battery life for these earbuds is good for this price range (6 to 8 hours, depending on whether or not you use ANC). As with most budget-priced wireless earbuds, maximum volume is OK but not great. Bass is above average for the $40 price. Static noise is very low. The Bluetooth connection has been very stable for me, even when I'm 30 feet away from my phone or in a different room in the house.

I can't give these earbuds 5 stars because I can easily buy better sound quality with more money, but these are solid 4 stars for value at the current $40 price.
text_fidelity_b: Donner Noise Cancelling Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.2 Earphones with 4 Mic Clear Calls, 12mm Drivers, App for Custom EQ, 32H Playtime, Fast Charging, Transparency - Dobuds ONE, Blue

I have three kinds of tripods, all consumer grade, nothing professional. As seen in my pictures, I compare the size of all three types. Farthest to the right is the standard tripod that doesn't fold down all that much, the middle is the compact tripod with a ball head and quick release, and the MOMAX is the farthest left.

From the pictures, you can see how much more compact the MOMAX tripod is. What you can't see is that due to its compact size, the footprint when fully deployed is also much smaller. It expands to a height of 56 inches, which is about chin or head height, which is tall enough for most portraits.

Each of my tripods serve a purpose but I foresee using the MOMAX most often because most of the time.

text_fidelity_a:
Apple AirPods Pro Long story short I lost my airpod pros. Saw these on major discount ($90 for Black Friday), and couldn't resist. So here's my take in four parts. Sound Quality. Noise Cancelling. Ambient pass through. Features.

Sound quality -- versus the airpod pros, these are almost identical in sound. The only difference is the beats buds are a touch bass heavy. It's good, punchy bass, but noticeably more than the pros which were more balanced with its lows. So if you're a bass head, or hip-hop enthusiast, the beats win hands down.

Noise cancelling -- now this could have to do with the shape of my ear, but I found the beats to actually be a step ABOVE in noise cancelling. My gf still has her airpods and I compared. The seal the beat creates, paired with its noise cancelling makes it seem like the world doesn't exist. Beats win for me in NC.

Ambient pass-through -- this is where the beats lose out. Their noise cancelling is too good. So even when you have transparency turned on the world sound a little muddied out, while with the airpods, if I had transparency on it was almost like I wasn't wearing them. I miss that alot. So if you are in an environment where you need to hear what people are saying without removing your buds then airpods might be your pick. It's not to say that beats mak you deaf or anything but things are just noticeably quieter in transparance vs airpods with its full clarity.

Features -- another loss for the beats. They don't work with the beats app so no equalizer function... why beats???? WHY?? So you'll have to go third party if you want to equalize. The beats also won't stop the music or video you're watching if one falls out. No biggy for me as I like that but some people might not. Other than that it has similar functionality to airpods. One click to pause, two to skip, etc. It doesn't auto switch between devices but does actually switch pretty similarly. Takes maybe two clicks to switch it to my mac. The pairing is a breeze with iphones. Just open the case next to your iphone and voila. It's paired.
text_fidelity_b: Apple AirPods Pro

text_fidelity_a: Roku 3 Streaming Media Player (2014 model) Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.
text_fidelity_b: Roku 3 Streaming Media Player (2014 model)

Nikon D810 FX-format Digital SLR Camera Body I have had this camera since July 2015 and I find that this camera to be the most incredible camera I have ever owned. I have owned the D700, D800, D600, D610 and still own the D750.The clarity and dynamic range surpasses all of my previous cameras, including my D750.
However, the D810 is very demanding on lenses. Inferior lenses will provide either inconsistent performance, or just plain horrendous results.
Edit: 11/29/2017: After over two years of regular use I have had no problems with this camera. I have never had to clean my sensor, and I change lenses frequently, as I most often use prime lenses. So, I don’t understand why so many people have the need to frequently to “dust off” or clean their sensor. Nor do I understand why some people complain about the fact that most of the outer shell is made of carbon fiber. For years I worked with advanced composites, and carbon fiber is not just cheap plastic, but is used in many high-tech products for its superior strength and light weight.

text_fidelity_a:
Incipio Highland Folio Case for Fire Phone, Black I had noticed that a huge percentage of people in the Middle East have folio cases for their phones, but I've seen so few here in the States that this was a big surprise to me. I like the idea a lot if you're keeping this in a purse or a pocket with a bunch of other stuff, but I've long ago reserved an entire pocket for my phone. In the case of a pocket, all this added texture actually makes it harder to get the phone out. And I can see the drawback others' mention about it not keeping itself shut; this could be a problem in the case of a purse with keys and all kinds of junk rolling around in there.

I really like the materials, however, to include the thin metal backing and the faux leather front. It stands up fine for a phone, but when you're already adding this amount of thickness, it seems like you could build some stopping points into the inside front cover. Of course that would mess up the credit card pocket. And speaking of that pocket, it seems like a good idea, if you can refrain from cramming so much into it that your phone becomes your wallet. I have another pocket on most pants, which I reserve for my wallet and keys; makes me wonder how other people live in such disorganization.

It's a pretty good quality product, and I suspect if you're looking for a folio case, you won't find one better. However, the point of the cover not staying shut is valid and maybe a reason to continue your research.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 12.2 (32GB, Black) There are more than enough helpful reviews, product specs and Q&A, so I am going to focus on this tablet for folks who are upgrading from another Android tablet, and especially another Samsung. I'll say up front that the biggest reason [for me, anyway] is the extra screen real estate and resolution.

I had a small surprise in that mine did not come with Amazon apps pre-installed like they did on my [[ASIN:B00D029NNA Samsung Galaxy Tab 3 (10.1-Inch, White) 2013 Model]] that it replaced. Locating the App Store application so I could install all of the applications that I have purchased was a bit of a hassle, but I finally got that resolved. Like my older Samsung tablet this one is a little less than spectacular when it comes to streaming music to a speaker via bluetooth. I do not know why Samsung cannot get it right on tablets because I have never experienced any issues streaming on my Note II and Note 3 phones.

Another issue of which you need to be aware is this tablet is thin and flexible. I knew that in advance and purchased a [[ASIN:B00KCDBD2E Samsung Galaxy Note Pro 12.2-inch Case Cover]], which in my opinion is one of the better cases for this tablet. The hard shell part of the case into which you insert the tablet provides a rigid casing that allows zero flex. No matter which case you ultimately select I strongly recommend that you get one.

You may have issues with some apps if you opt to install an SD card to expand your storage, or if you are moving an SD card from another tablet to this one. The KitKat version of the operating system will not write to SD cards under certain conditions. There is a free fix called SD KitKat Fixer by JRummy Apps that you can get from the Play Store. I highly recommend it. As a side note, I had no issues with this SD card: [[ASIN:B00N2ROG9O PNY Turbo Performance 64GB High Speed MicroSDXC Class 10 UHS-1]]. It is an inexpensive way to max out your memory. I have heard that this tablet will work with 128GB cards, but I have not tested any so cannot say for sure.

If you are accustomed to Samsung's user interface you will feel right at home. For me, after the little challenges I mentioned above I was fully up and operational on this tablet in a few hours. A lot of that time was reinstalling purchased apps from Amazon and the Play Store, tweaking my settings so that they mirrored those on my Tab 10.1 (which are identical to my Note 3 phone), and this feels as comfortable as an old shoe. A much larger old shoe to be sure, and it's incredible how much extra screen space you get going from 10.1 to 12.2.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 12.2 (32GB, Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black) For the non-professional photographer looking to get high-quality images in a variety of settings, this camera works great. I did a little experiment to see how it performed by taking it with me to Europe along with a much more expensive semi-professional Nikon (D3100). Here are the results:

Advantages:
-With our limited time, my camera was able to take a variety of shots (panoramic, zoom, close-up) quickly and easily while the Nikon could only take limited kinds because of the need to bring several lenses and because of the complexity (sometimes) of setting up a given shot
-Because it was small, I didn't have to lug around a big camera bag, which also had the potential of getting a little too much unwanted attention
-One feature I really enjoyed was the two simultaneous flash/no flash shot which gives you the same picture with and without flash, letting you choose later which you prefer
-Didn't need more than one lens
-With city shots of architecture, my camera fared better with its versatility

Disadvantages:
-In the mountains, the Nikon did better, capturing color and clarity/detail. In my shots, the trees looked less defined from high up. Also, his zoom lens was able to capture much more detail than my camera.
-Nature shots and portraits have slightly duller colors, missing something the other camera was able to capture
-There was slightly more blur in shots with movement with this camera

Conclusion:
For the price, this camera performed much better than I expected and was not as much of a hassle as our semi-professional camera, so for most people, this is not only going to be a better value, but less frustrating and cumbersome. For the professional, this is obviously not the best choice, but this isn't being marketed as a professional camera. This is a great family and vacation camera that everyone can use, and that still yields quality images with plenty of artistic integrity.
Great little camera, and fun to use!

**see pics for some examples of how this camera performed**
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin 4.3-Inch Carrying Case Bought this for the 750 because it didn't come with a case. A similar (smaller) case came with my 360 and I didn't think this purchase through. After using it and comparing the other cases out there, I would buy a different case.

This slipcase for the 750 fits tight. That's good. The Nuvi won't slip out. But because the 750's on/off switch is now a slider on the top left corner, if you slide it into the case naturally (unit in your right hand, case in your left) the switch rubs against the case. When you pull the unit out, it "automatically" turns on. Thus if you were to pull the unit out partially then push it back in, you could turn it on and not know it.

The solution is to invert the Nuvi so its switch will be at the open end of the case after it's in the case. That way you can see the switch's on/off position and verify it's not on.

More practical issues:

Pros:

- Nicely made: very high quality

- Very compact

- Adequate protection against rattling inside a glove compartment or briefcase

- Good basic case

Cons:

- It can accidentally turn the unit on

- It's black: can't find it easily in the dark buried at the bottom of my shoulder bag when traveling. Experienced this with the 360's case. And if it falls on the floor of a rental car at night, good luck trying to find it. Wish it came in natural leather color.

- Offers no protection while hand holding the unit while walking

The [[ASIN:B0012MI7N2 Garmin Nuvi 800 Series Carrying Case]] case is a wallet style that flips open to reveal the screen. It stays on the unit during use and offers some protection if you dropped your Nuvi on the sidewalk while walking. Downside with that unit appears to be that the cover flap does not latch, allowing the case to flip open in a briefcase and the screen to be scratched by other junk. And it's also black and can get lost on a car floor.

Another alternate is one of the many zippered semi-rigid or neoprene cases.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin 4.3-Inch Carrying Case

text_fidelity_a:
Arctic Cooling P311-BK Bluetooth Stereo Headset with Microphone Overall, these are a decent pair of bluetooth earphones. The build quality is good for the price, with sturdy arms that fold so the headphones can be stowed easily in a carry case (or pocket). The ear padding is on the thin side, but there's enough to maintain comfort for a reasonable amount of wear time.

The sound quality is more than decent for the price. They won't stun you with huge bass and crisp mid and upper ranges, but for general all-purpose listening (e.g., music, movies, etc.) they get the job done well.

It paired easily with a Fire and a Nexus. The operating range is quite good - I had no problems maintaining a connection from the opposite side of a large room (about 20 or so feet).

Misses center on two issues: controls and the case. The controls are small and unobtrusive, which is nice from an aesthetic standpoint - the headset casing looks sleek. However, in actual usage, it can be hard to find the proper button by touch alone. Some type of tactile cue would have been nice to ensure you get to the right button each and every time.

I also think the case could have been better. While it's stylish (sort of a triangular shape) with a crease in the cover that adds visual interest, there's no mesh or straps on the inside to hold the headphones and/or cables. The end result is that while the case looks nicer than others I've used, it's not as practical or functional. I find that to be a significant issue since I use these type of headphones away from home (e.g., at the gym, while exercising, etc.) and the carry case gets used a lot.

Given that these are priced the same or a bit higher than other similar bluetooth headsets, these misses warrant dropping the rating by one star. However, they remain a good choice if you're looking for a generally inexpensive set of headphones - they sound pretty good, seems to be well-made, and have a good operating range.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Arctic Cooling P311-BK Bluetooth Stereo Headset with Microphone

text_fidelity_a:
Cobra RX680 Waterproof Walkie Talkies for Adults - Rechargeable, 60 Preset Channels, Long Range 38-Mile Two-Way Radio Set (2-Pack),Black and Orange So many things I love about these. These appear to be as rugged and well built as I'd expected from a brand name like Cobra. I love that they include a flashlight, and especially that the units are USB rechargeable! Such a convenient way to power things these days, I wish more electronics ditched the AAA batteries thing like this!
The range might be a bit exaggerated, but to be fair I live in a very wooded area surrounded by hills and valleys. I found that around my neighborhood it worked great but if I went a few miles away, the sound was mostly just unintelligible crackling. We could still hear that someone was trying to say something, but that's it.
On the flip side, we started hearing someone else's conversation the next day... we were just testing it so we didn't bother changing the default channel, and it turns out someone else must have gotten some talkies on the same default frequencies. I have no idea how close they were, but my kids pointed out that someone was talking and we didn't press any buttons and then we all heard it. "Dad? Do I need to come in? I'm playing outside", and then a few seconds later "ok, but don't ride into the street". Then some clicks of singing and other noises- clearly someone else communicating with THEIR kid was coming through to us. I pressed the talk button and said "Hi- this is the default frequency for these walkie talkies, so we should both probably change them!" and then promptly picked another channel. So, that's kind of neat because I have no idea where these other people were, we live in a pretty urban area with houses spread out and I know it wasn't someone from my block. Yet we heard them clear as day. So, I'd say these are pretty good at what they do, but maybe don't rely on the full extent of their listed range.
text_fidelity_b: Cobra RX680 Waterproof Walkie Talkies for Adults - Rechargeable, 60 Preset Channels, Long Range 38-Mile Two-Way Radio Set (2-Pack),Black and Orange

text_fidelity_a:
Monoprice Blackbird 4K 3x1 HDMI 1.4 Switch - Compact, HDCP 2.2, Built-in Equalizer, 4K 30Hz, YCbCr 4:4:4, 18Gbps (Compatible with PS4/5 Xbox Apple TV Fire Stick Roku Blu-Ray Player) Since we mounted our TV we like to use as few chords as possible. This way they are neatly tucked along the wall and down into the entertainment center where all our entertainment equipment is housed. So the main HDMI cable runs down but of course we have more components that require a cable than the one connected to the TV. Our solution? A signal splitter. Thankfully, we have only three output connections so this one seemed perfect. Plus, it touts 4k signal, even though most pre-4k HDMI boxes should be fine, but it's nice to have that in the title just in case.

What I use this mostly for is the cable box and a couple of video game systems. As for the cable box, seems to work fine; no dropped signals that I've noticed, nor any degradation in quality. As for game consoles, I have the PS3 and the Wii U hooked up to it. SAme: no noticeable quality degradation nor input lag.
Now, to put it to the real test, I hooked up some retro consoles that have been modded to output native HDMI; that means they'll be HDMI with no lag. Considering I have this and two HDMI cables connecting the console to the TV, I was curious to see if there truly was any lag.
With older games, timing is everything, especially on the 8-bit consoles with platformers and fighters, like the NES. From what I could tell, there was absolutely no lag, not to mention signal loss. The buttons responded as though I were using a normal NES on a CRT.

So yeah, I'm pretty satisfied. It's a bit light and doesn't have heavy pads on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around. With so many cables, and the ability to use the remote control, it should be a bit more stable on the surface.
I haven't used the remote as the detections are instant. No need to manually switch the inputs, at least from my experience. Also, I didn't need to use the power adapter; the power from the HDMI cables seemed to be sufficient, and the detection was not complicated by the lack of adapter. Weird.
text_fidelity_b: Monoprice Blackbird 4K 3x1 HDMI 1.4 Switch - Compact, HDCP 2.2, Built-in Equalizer, 4K 30Hz, YCbCr 4:4:4, 18Gbps (Compatible with PS4/5 Xbox Apple TV Fire Stick Roku Blu-Ray Player)

FLAGTOP 7 in 1 USB C Hub for Universal Devices, Support 4K HDMI/PD 3.0 / USB 3.0 / 2USB 2.0 / SD/Micro SD/TF, USB Type C Dongle Hub (02A) I have a 2017 MacBook Pro with 4 Thunderbolt/USB C ports. Of course almost every peripheral I use is USB 2.0/3.0, so I have adapters everywhere and can never find one when I need it, or don’t have enough ports to plug in everything I want to use.

So this USB C Hub from Flagtop is super handy to have around. I use it to connect a second monitor (HDMI port), an external mouse/keyboard (USB 2.0 ports), and the power cable (USB C port).

I like that the USB 2.0/USB 3.0 ports have a little space between each one. This makes them usable even if you have a thick thumb drive or cable plugged in.

I had to have the ports on my laptop replaced because they loosened up over time, so I like that I can reduce wear on the new ports by unplugging the hub to disconnect everything.

The port runs warm. It’s hot to the touch; my desk feels warm underneath it.

I do wish the cable for the hub was longer. If I have my laptop on a stand, the hub dangles from one of the ports. The cable is about 5.5 inches, and if I have several things plugged into it, I feel like that’s a lot of weight to have hanging off a single port on the side of my laptop.
